breakfast.name: Birchermuesli (Original Swiss Muesli)
ingredients: Rolled oats (soaked overnight in water or milk)
Lemon juice (1 tbsp -- the Bircher secret ingredient)
Apple (grated -- the main ingredient, not decoration)
instructions: Birchermuesli was invented by Swiss physician Maximilian Bircher-Brenner around 1900
He developed it as a health dish at his Zurich sanatorium -- it was prescribed to patients
The original Birchermuesli: mostly grated apple, very little oats
The recipe: one tablespoon of oats soaked overnight in water with lemon juice
Then one tablespoon of condensed milk, one grated apple, one tablespoon nuts
The lemon juice is essential -- it prevents the apple from browning and adds acidity
The apple is the dominant ingredient: grated on the large side of a grater
The oats are a backdrop, not the main event -- a common misunderstanding
Bircher-Brenner believed in raw food and plant-based diets -- revolutionary for 1900
Modern birchermuesli: adapted with more oats, yoghurt, and fruit -- more substantial
The Zurich Paradeplatz banks serve birchermuesli -- the Swiss financial capital breakfast
breakfast.description: The original Swiss health dish, invented by physician Maximilian Bircher-Brenner around 1900 for his Zurich sanatorium patients -- oats soaked overnight in water with lemon juice, mixed with grated apple (the dominant ingredient), condensed milk, and hazelnuts. The lemon juice prevents browning and adds acidity. The original is mostly apple with very little oat; modern versions invert this.

breakfast.name: Zurcher Bread and Butter Breakfast
ingredients: Zopf (Swiss braided bread -- egg-and-butter enriched yeast bread)
Swiss honey (Waldhonig = forest honey, or Berghonig = mountain honey)
Swiss cheese (Emmentaler or Gruyere -- thin slices)
instructions: The Swiss breakfast is simple and centered on quality ingredients
Zopf: the Swiss braided Sunday bread -- enriched with butter and egg, golden, glossy
The name Zopf means braid -- the two strands woven into the characteristic Swiss bread shape
Zopf is Sunday bread: it signals the week has ended and the weekend begun
Swiss butter has a higher fat content than most European butter -- 84%+ butterfat
The Swiss mountain pastures produce exceptional milk -- the fat quality is noticeable
Swiss honey: Waldhonig (forest honey, from honeydew) and Berghonig (mountain flower honey)
Emmentaler or Gruyere in thin slices: Switzerland has 450+ registered cheese varieties
The Swiss breakfast is high-quality simplicity -- quality of each ingredient matters
Swiss bread culture: each canton and valley has traditional bread forms
breakfast.description: Swiss quality-ingredient breakfast -- Zopf (Swiss braided Sunday bread, enriched with butter and egg) with high-fat Swiss butter (84%+ butterfat from mountain-pastured cows), Swiss honey (forest or mountain flower), and thin-sliced Emmentaler or Gruyere. The Swiss breakfast is high-quality simplicity: the quality of each ingredient is the statement.

breakfast.name: Polenta Mattutina (Ticino Morning Polenta)
ingredients: Water or milk (half-half for breakfast version)
Honey or sugar (for the sweet version)
instructions: Polenta mattutina is the breakfast polenta of the Ticino canton -- Italian-speaking Switzerland
Ticino: the southern canton below the Alps, bordering Italy and speaking Italian
The food culture of Ticino is distinctly Italian -- polenta, risotto, wine from the Merlot tradition
The breakfast polenta: made with milk (softer, creamier than the savory version)
Cooked with constant stirring -- polenta requires attention and a wooden spoon
Served with warm milk poured over -- the polenta-in-milk is the Ticinese way
Sweetened with honey or sugar: the sweet morning polenta
This is distinct from German-speaking Switzerland: the same country, a different food culture
The Röstigraben (rösti ditch): the cultural divide between German and French/Italian Switzerland
Below the Alps, you eat polenta; above the Alps, you eat rösti
breakfast.description: Ticinese breakfast polenta -- Ticino is Italian-speaking Switzerland, south of the Alps, and the food culture is distinctly Italian. Coarse cornmeal stirred with milk until soft and creamy, served with warm milk poured over and honey. This is Swiss but it could be Lombard: the same Alps, a different food culture on each side. The Röstigraben (cultural divide) is visible at breakfast.

breakfast.name: Cafe Complet (Swiss Complete Coffee Breakfast)
ingredients: Croissant (or gipfeli -- the Swiss butter croissant)
instructions: Cafe complet (German: Kaffee komplett) is the Swiss hotel and cafe breakfast
The concept: a complete breakfast ordered from a Swiss cafe in one phrase
Coffee + croissant (or gipfeli) + butter + jam: the package
Gipfeli: the Swiss butter croissant -- slightly different from French, less flaky, more bready
The Swiss coffee tradition: not Italian espresso culture, not French cafe au lait
Swiss filter coffee is strong but milder than Italian espresso
The term cafe complet communicates everything: the Swiss efficiency in one phrase
Swiss cafe culture: the Konditorei (patisserie-cafe) is the institution
The Sprüngli Cafe in Zurich and the Confiserie Schober: the Swiss cafe institution
Cafe complet in the French-speaking part: the tradition is more French, the coffee more cafe
breakfast.description: Swiss cafe breakfast -- coffee + Gipfeli (Swiss butter croissant, slightly less flaky than French) + butter + jam ordered as a single package with the phrase cafe complet. The Swiss Konditorei is the breakfast and afternoon institution. Swiss filter coffee is strong but milder than Italian espresso. The Gipfeli vs French croissant: the Röstigraben visible in the bakery.

lunch.name: Zürcher Geschnetzeltes (Zurich Veal in Cream)
ingredients: Veal (thinly sliced -- the original, though chicken is used today)
instructions: Zurcher Geschnetzeltes is the Zurich dish -- and arguably the most internationally known Swiss dish
The name: Zurcher = from Zurich; Geschnetzeltes = cut into thin strips
Veal cut into thin strips: the technique -- the thin cut is the dish
Fry in butter at high heat -- the veal browns in seconds, do not overcook
The mushrooms: cooked in the same pan, adding earthiness
Deglaze with white wine -- the wine lifts the pan residue
The cream poured in -- reduced to a rich, velvet sauce
Served exclusively with rösti -- the Zurich combination is inseparable
The rösti is the potato cake that represents German-Swiss culture
Zurcher Geschnetzeltes at the Zurich Kronenhalle: the institution
The Kronenhalle: the famous Zurich restaurant with Picasso and Miro on the walls
Often made with kidneys (Zurich veal and kidney): the original version
lunch.description: The Zurich dish -- veal cut into thin strips and seared quickly in butter, mushrooms added, deglazed with white wine, cream reduced to a velvet sauce. Served exclusively with rösti (Swiss potato cake). The Zurich combination is inseparable: Geschnetzeltes + rösti. The Kronenhalle restaurant in Zurich serves the canonical version under Miro and Picasso paintings.

lunch.name: Fondue (Swiss Cheese Fondue)
ingredients: Dry white wine (Fendant or other Swiss white)
instructions: Fondue is the Swiss national communal dish -- melted cheese and bread
The classic fondue: moitie-moitie (half-half): Gruyere + Vacherin Fribourgeois
The caquelon (fondue pot): a specific earthenware vessel rubbed with garlic inside
The wine: dry Swiss white wine (Fendant from Valais is the classic) goes into the pot
Heat the wine, add grated cheese gradually, stir constantly in a figure-8 motion
Cornstarch mixed with kirsch: added to stabilize the fondue against separation
The fondue must stay warm on the rechaud (spirit burner) throughout the meal
The bread: stale bread is the traditional dipper -- day-old bread grips the cheese better
The tradition: if you drop your bread in the fondue, you buy the next round
The croute: the crispy cheese crust on the bottom of the pot at the end -- the prize
Fondue is winter, mountain, and communal eating -- the Swiss mountain hut tradition
The skiing tradition: fondue after the slopes
lunch.description: Swiss national communal dish -- moitie-moitie (half Gruyere, half Vacherin Fribourgeois) melted in dry Swiss white wine (Fendant from Valais) with cornstarch and a splash of kirsch, kept warm in an earthenware caquelon over a spirit burner. Bread cubes dipped in. The croute (crispy cheese crust on the bottom at the end) is the prize. Winter, mountain, and community eating.

lunch.name: Rosti (Swiss Potato Cake)
ingredients: Optional additions: bacon (lardons), Gruyere on top, fried egg
instructions: Rösti is the Swiss German potato cake -- the emblem of German-speaking Switzerland
The Röstigraben (rösti ditch) is the cultural-linguistic divide: German Switzerland eats rösti; French does not
The key question: boiled potatoes (pre-cooked) or raw? Both schools exist
Boiled-then-grated: the potatoes hold together better, the texture is softer
Raw grated: the exterior crispier, the interior denser
Grate the potatoes, squeeze out as much moisture as possible
Melt generous butter in a non-stick pan -- the butter is the flavor carrier
The rösti goes in as a single cake -- pressed flat, then cooked without stirring
Medium heat until the bottom is golden and crispy -- the crust is essential
Flip onto a plate and slide back into the pan -- cook the other side
The rösti should slide freely in the pan if the butter is sufficient
Served alongside Zurcher Geschnetzeltes, fried eggs, or simply with applesauce
lunch.description: The German-Swiss potato cake -- grated potatoes (raw or pre-boiled: two schools) pressed into a cake in generous butter, cooked without stirring until one side is deeply golden and crispy, then flipped. The Röstigraben (rösti ditch) is the cultural divide: German-speaking Switzerland eats rösti; French Switzerland does not. Served alongside Zurcher Geschnetzeltes or simply with applesauce.

lunch.name: Raclette
ingredients: Raclette cheese (a wheel or pre-cut slices -- from Valais canton, Switzerland)
instructions: Raclette is the other great Swiss fondue-family dish -- but more ancient
Raclette: the name comes from racler (to scrape) -- the melted cheese is scraped off
Original raclette: a half-wheel of raclette cheese held before an open fire
The exposed face melts and is scraped onto a plate with boiled potatoes
Modern raclette: electric raclette machines with individual small pans (caquelons)
Each person melts their own cheese in the small pan under the heating element
The pickled gherkins and pearl onions are essential -- the acid cuts through the fat
The boiled potatoes absorb the melted cheese -- this is the combination
Raclette is Valais cheese: the high alpine canton of southwestern Switzerland
The Valais raclette has a PDO designation -- authentic Valais only
Raclette is the Swiss farmhouse dinner -- served with white wine (Fendant)
lunch.description: The ancient Swiss mountain dish -- a half-wheel of Valais raclette cheese melted before an open fire (or under an electric element) and scraped onto boiled potatoes, with pickled gherkins (cornichons) and pearl onions to cut the fat. Raclette means to scrape. Valais canton PDO cheese. White Fendant wine alongside. More ancient than fondue; equally Swiss.

lunch.name: Berner Platte (Bernese Mixed Plate)
instructions: Berner Platte is the Bernese (canton Bern) mixed smoked meat plate
Bern: the Swiss federal capital, in the heart of German-speaking Switzerland
The plate celebrates the Bernese tradition of cold-smoked and air-cured meats
Berner Trockenfleisch (Bernese dried beef): the most prized element
The air-drying of beef in the cold Bernese Mitteland winds is the traditional technique
Each meat is cooked separately then arranged on the plate
The sauerkraut: the German-Swiss fermented cabbage, slightly different from German
The Berner Platte is served at special occasions -- not an everyday dish
Canton Bern pride: the Berner Platte is the edible emblem of Bernese culture
The smoked meats and dried beef tradition reflects the need to preserve through Alpine winters
lunch.description: Bernese mixed smoked meat plate -- a celebration of the Bernese canton cold-smoking and air-curing tradition: Trockenfleisch (dried beef), smoked tongue, Bernese sausage, and pork knuckle, served with sauerkraut, green beans, and boiled potatoes. Bern is the Swiss federal capital; the Berner Platte is the edible emblem of Bernese cultural pride.

dinner.name: Choucroute Garnie (Alsatian-Swiss Sauerkraut with Meats)
ingredients: White wine (Riesling or Pinot Gris from Alsace or Swiss German)
Juniper berries, bay leaf, caraway seeds
instructions: Choucroute garnie is shared between Alsace (France) and Basel/German Switzerland
The border region between France and Switzerland has always shared this dish
Sauerkraut (fermented cabbage) braised in Riesling with juniper and caraway
The juniper berries are the flavoring note that distinguishes choucroute
The meats: smoked sausages, smoked pork loin, smoked ham -- all cooked with the sauerkraut
The meats are added in sequence: longer-cooking meats first, sausages last
The sauerkraut should be slightly soft but still with texture
Served on a large platter: sauerkraut mounded with meats arranged on top
Boiled potatoes alongside: the starch
Dijon mustard for the sausages: mandatory
dinner.description: Basel and Alsatian shared dish -- sauerkraut braised in Riesling with juniper berries, caraway, and onion, with smoked sausages, pork loin, and ham hock cooked in the sauerkraut, served on a platter with boiled potatoes and Dijon mustard. Shared between French Alsace and German-Swiss Basel: the Rhine is the border but the food is the same.

dinner.name: Maluns (Graubunden Potato Dish)
ingredients: Potatoes (boiled the day before -- leftovers essential)
Butter (generous -- brown butter is the flavor)
instructions: Maluns is the Graubunden (Grisons) potato dish -- Romansh-speaking Switzerland
Graubunden: the largest Swiss canton by area, with three official languages
The Romansh tradition: maluns is Romansh-influenced mountain cooking
Maluns requires leftover potatoes: cooked the day before and cooled completely
Grate the cold potatoes coarsely -- the cold potato grates differently
The flour: a small amount mixed with the grated potato
Cooked in generous brown butter -- the butter browns and flavors the potato crust
The technique: the potato mixture is worked in the pan until small pieces form
The result: small crispy-edged potato pieces, not a unified cake (different from rösti)
Served exclusively with warm applesauce: the sweet-salty-fat combination
Maluns is obscure outside Graubunden -- locals consider it their own treasure
dinner.description: Graubunden (Romansh-Swiss) leftover potato dish -- cold boiled potatoes from the day before grated and mixed with flour, cooked in brown butter until small crispy-edged pieces form (not a cake like rösti: the butter and technique create loose, crunchy morsels). Served exclusively with warm applesauce. Obscure outside Graubunden; locals consider it their own food treasure.

dinner.name: Halves (Bernese Half-Roast Chicken)
instructions: Half-roast chicken (halves) is an everyday Swiss dinner -- practical and satisfying
Switzerland has strong butchery and meat quality traditions from the alpine farming regions
The chicken: Swiss free-range chicken from the highland farms when possible
Rubbed with butter, salt, paprika, and herbs -- the simple Swiss preparation
Roasted until the skin is golden and crispy
Swiss roast chicken is served with rösti or potato gratin
The Swiss approach to everyday food: quality ingredients, simple preparation
Halves (Halbhähnchen): sold at Swiss markets and Metzgerei (butcher shops) to take away
The rotisserie chicken at Swiss markets is a Swiss tradition
dinner.description: Swiss everyday roast chicken -- half-chicken rubbed with butter, salt, paprika, and Swiss herbs, roasted until golden-crispy. The Swiss approach: quality free-range chicken, simple preparation. Served with rösti or potato gratin. Sold at Swiss markets and butcher shops as takeaway.

dinner.name: Tessiner Risotto (Ticino Risotto)
ingredients: Arborio or Carnaroli rice (short-grain Italian risotto rice)
Dry white wine (Ticino Merlot bianco or similar)
Vegetable or chicken broth (hot, kept simmering)
Saffron (optional -- Milanese style) or white truffle shaving (luxurious)
instructions: Tessiner Risotto is from the Ticino canton -- Italian-Swiss cuisine
Ticino uses Italian cooking techniques but Swiss ingredients and sensibility
The risotto technique: toasting the rice in butter (tostatura) before any liquid
Deglazing with white wine -- the wine steams and is absorbed
Adding hot broth ladle by ladle, stirring constantly
The mantecatura: the finishing step -- beating cold butter and cheese into the hot rice
This final beating creates the creamy, emulsified texture of great risotto
The rice should be al dente -- firm to the bite at the center
The texture: all'onda (wavy) -- the risotto flows like a wave when the plate is tilted
Ticino is Italy in Switzerland: wine, olive oil, pasta, and risotto south of the Alps
dinner.description: Ticinese Italian-Swiss risotto -- short-grain rice toasted in butter, deglazed with white wine, built ladle by ladle with hot broth while stirring, finished with cold butter and aged cheese beaten in (mantecatura) for a creamy, wavy consistency (all'onda). Ticino is Italy in Switzerland: wine, olive oil, and risotto south of the Alps. The same technique as Milanese risotto, but with Swiss sensibility.

dinner.name: Alplermagronen (Alpine Mac and Cheese)
ingredients: Potatoes (waxy -- diced, cooked in the pasta water)
instructions: Alplermagronen is the Swiss mountain mac and cheese -- the alpine hut dish
The name: Alpler = alpine herdsman, magronen = macaroni
Made by herdsmen in the Swiss alpine summer huts (Alp) with available ingredients
The combination: pasta + potato + Swiss cheese + cream
The potato cooks with the pasta -- they share cooking water
The cheese melts through the pasta and potato when mixed
The cream makes everything unctuous and binding
The caramelized onion rings on top: the golden, sweet, crunchy topping
Served with cold applesauce -- the sweet-salty contrast is the point
Alplermagronen is Swiss mountain comfort food at its most direct
In autumn when the herdsmen descend from the Alp: the Alpabzug festival serves alplermagronen
dinner.description: Swiss alpine mac and cheese -- macaroni and diced potatoes cooked together, mixed with generous Gruyere or Appenzeller, cream, and caramelized onion rings on top, served with cold applesauce. Made by alpine herdsmen in Swiss summer mountain huts from available ingredients. Pasta + potato + alpine cheese + cream: the alpine pantry in one bowl. Autumn Alpabzug (herd descent) festival food.

snacks.name: Swiss Cheese Platter
ingredients: Emmentaler (the holey Swiss cheese -- mild, nutty)
Gruyere (harder, nuttier, more complex than Emmentaler)
Appenzeller (the spiciest Swiss cheese -- rubbed with herbal brine)
Raclette cheese (the melting cheese, also good cold)
instructions: Switzerland has 450+ registered cheese varieties -- the greatest cheese nation by variety per capita
The Swiss cheese tradition comes from alpine summer cheese production
The herdsmen drove cattle to high alpine pastures in summer -- the milk was too abundant to transport
So they made cheese in the alpine huts -- the wheel is the transportable preserved milk
Emmentaler: the most internationally famous Swiss cheese -- large wheels, characteristic holes
Gruyere: harder, more complex, longer aged -- the Swiss cooking and eating cheese
Appenzeller: rubbed with a secret herbal-spiced brine -- the most distinctive flavor
The 450+ varieties reflect the diversity of Swiss valleys and mountain traditions
snacks.description: Switzerland greatest product -- 450+ registered cheese varieties from alpine summer production (herdsmen made cheese in mountain huts because summer milk was too abundant to transport, and wheels are the portable preserved form). Emmentaler, Gruyere, Appenzeller, and Raclette are the internationally known varieties. The diversity reflects the variety of Swiss valleys and alpine traditions.

snacks.name: Toblerone
ingredients: Toblerone chocolate (Swiss -- milk chocolate with honey-almond nougat, triangular shape)
instructions: Toblerone is the iconic Swiss chocolate from Bern
Created in 1908 by Theodor Tobler and Emil Baumann
The triangular shape: inspired by the Matterhorn or the Haute de Cry mountain -- disputed
The distinctive segmented bar: each triangle-peak section breaks off individually
Milk chocolate with Swiss honey and almond nougat pieces throughout
The nougat gives Toblerone its characteristic chewy-sweet contrast with the chocolate
Switzerland is the world leading chocolate per-capita consumer (10kg per person per year)
Swiss chocolate quality: strict regulations, high cocoa butter content, Swiss milk
Other Swiss chocolate institutions: Lindt, Nestlé (Swiss origin), Cailler
Toblerone is sold in every Swiss airport -- the international Swiss food ambassador
snacks.description: Switzerland iconic chocolate from Bern, created 1908 -- milk chocolate with Swiss honey and almond nougat in the triangular segmented bar inspired by the Alpine peak silhouette. Switzerland is the world leading chocolate per-capita consumer (10kg/person/year). Toblerone is sold in every Swiss airport as the international food ambassador of Switzerland.

snacks.name: Landjager (Swiss Dried Sausage)
ingredients: Landjager (Swiss dried sausage -- pressed flat, air-cured)
instructions: Landjager is the Swiss dried sausage -- the portable alpine food
The name: Landsjager = country hunter (Jager = hunter)
The sausage is pressed flat into its characteristic rectangular shape during curing
The flatness allows it to fit into pockets -- the hiker and soldier food
Made from beef and pork with black pepper, caraway, garlic, and red wine
Air-cured for weeks until the surface is dark, almost black, the texture firm
Eaten cold, sliced or bitten directly -- no cooking required
Landjager has been carried by Swiss soldiers for centuries
Still sold at Swiss markets, butcher shops, and mountain huts
The Swiss military tradition: landjager and army knife in every soldier backpack
snacks.description: Swiss portable alpine sausage -- beef and pork with black pepper and caraway, pressed flat into a rectangular shape (pocket-sized) and air-cured until firm and dark. The name means country hunter. Carried by Swiss soldiers for centuries and still sold at mountain huts. No cooking required; bitten or sliced directly. The Swiss portable food tradition.

snacks.name: Leckerli (Basel Spiced Biscuit)
instructions: Leckerli (or Lebkuchen of Basel) is the Basel spiced biscuit -- Basel specialty
Basel: the Swiss Rhine city with a long spice trade history
The spice trade came up the Rhine from the Mediterranean -- Basel was the major junction
This spice access gave Basel its exceptional spiced biscuit tradition
The dough: honey, flour, mixed spice, candied peel, almonds, kirsch
Honey-based dough keeps the leckerli moist for weeks -- the keeping quality
Baked as a single large sheet then cut into rectangular pieces when still warm
Glazed with icing sugar while hot -- the glaze sets to a thin, sweet crust
Leckerli improve with age -- they are traditionally made weeks in advance
Sold in Basel bakeries and sold as a Basel souvenir in red tin boxes
Christmas in Basel: leckerli production reaches its peak in December
snacks.description: Basel spiced honey biscuit -- honey dough with mixed spice (cinnamon, cloves, anise, cardamom), candied orange and lemon peel, almonds, and kirsch, baked in a sheet and cut into rectangles when warm, glazed with icing sugar. Basel had access to the spice trade via the Rhine; this spice access made Basel exceptional for baked spices. Improves with age. Sold in red tin boxes as a Basel souvenir.

desserts.name: Vermicelles (Chestnut Vermicelli)
ingredients: Chestnut puree (cooked chestnuts pureed -- or canned)
instructions: Vermicelles is the Swiss chestnut dessert -- a specific Swiss creation
The name: vermicelli = little worms -- the chestnut puree is pressed through a sieve into worm shapes
The chestnuts: traditionally from the Swiss Margueria (Ticino chestnut forests)
Ticino produces excellent chestnuts -- the chestnut forests in the river valleys
The chestnut puree is pressed through a sieve or special vermicelles press
The result: a mound of thin chestnut threads (the worms/vermicelles)
Topped with whipped cream -- the cold cream against the earthy chestnut
Vermicelles is served at Swiss autumn fairs and markets
The marronifest (chestnut festival) in Ticino: vermicelles and roasted chestnuts
The Swiss autumn dessert -- appearing in October-November when chestnuts ripen
desserts.description: Swiss chestnut dessert -- chestnut puree pressed through a sieve or special press to create thin thread-like worms (vermicelli), mounded and topped with whipped cream. The chestnuts come from Ticino chestnut forests. A Swiss autumn creation, appearing at October-November markets and fairs. The marronifest (chestnut festival) in Ticino is the high point of vermicelles season.

desserts.name: Zuger Kirschtorte (Cherry Brandy Cake)
ingredients: Swiss kirsch (cherry brandy from Zug -- essential)
Pink sugar glaze (the pink color is the Zuger Kirschtorte signature)
instructions: Zuger Kirschtorte is the cake of the Zug canton -- named after the city and its kirsch
Zug canton: small, wealthy, and home to exceptional kirsch production
Zuger kirsch: double-distilled cherry brandy from wild cherries -- the finest Swiss kirsch
The cake: genoise sponge layers soaked with kirsch, filled with vanilla buttercream
The exterior: wrapped in marzipan, then glazed with pink sugar glaze
The pink color is the visual identity of the Zuger Kirschtorte
The kirsch soaking: the sponge absorbs the cherry brandy -- the dominant flavor
A properly made Zuger Kirschtorte has a strong kirsch presence
Made and sold in Zug pastry shops: the local pride cake
Visitors to Zug are expected to bring home a Zuger Kirschtorte
desserts.description: The cake of Zug canton -- genoise sponge layers soaked with Zug kirsch (the finest Swiss double-distilled cherry brandy), filled with vanilla buttercream, wrapped in marzipan and glazed pink (the visual identity). A properly made version has a strong kirsch presence. Made in Zug pastry shops; visitors are expected to bring one home.

desserts.name: Schoggi Fondue (Chocolate Fondue)
ingredients: Dipping items: strawberries, banana slices, marshmallows, dried apricots, cake cubes
instructions: Chocolate fondue is the Swiss dessert gift to the world
Switzerland: both the fondue tradition and the chocolate tradition meeting in one dish
Melt dark Swiss chocolate in warm cream -- the ganache is the base
Add kirsch or Grand Marnier -- the alcohol adds depth and prevents crystallization
Kept warm in a fondue pot or small caquelon
Dipping items: anything that benefits from being coated in warm dark chocolate
Strawberries: the classic -- the acidity against the chocolate
Banana: the tropical sweetness coated in dark Swiss chocolate
The chocolate fondue is the Swiss social dessert -- communal, playful, interactive
The same social rules as cheese fondue: drop the item, face the consequence
desserts.description: Swiss dessert fondue -- dark Swiss chocolate (70%+) melted in warm cream with kirsch, kept warm in a caquelon for communal dipping of strawberries, banana slices, and cake cubes. Switzerland combines two traditions: fondue and chocolate. The same social rules as cheese fondue: drop your item, face the consequence. The Swiss social dessert.

drinks.name: Rivella (Swiss Whey Drink)
ingredients: Rivella (Swiss carbonated soft drink made from milk whey)
instructions: Rivella is the Swiss national soft drink -- unique to Switzerland
Made from milk whey (the liquid byproduct of cheese production)
Switzerland makes huge quantities of cheese -- the whey is abundant
Rivella transforms the whey into a light, carbonated, slightly sweet drink
The flavor is unlike anything else: slightly dairy, slightly fruity, clean
Three varieties: red Rivella (original), blue (lower sugar), green (with green tea)
Rivella is more popular in Switzerland than Coca-Cola
The Swiss relationship with milk and dairy extends to their soft drink
Rivella is taken seriously in Switzerland -- part of the Swiss identity
Difficult to describe to foreigners: a carbonated dairy drink that tastes nothing like dairy
drinks.description: The Swiss national soft drink -- carbonated drink made from milk whey (the byproduct of Swiss cheese production). Switzerland makes enough cheese to produce abundant whey; Rivella transforms it into a light, clean, slightly sweet fizzy drink unlike anything else. More popular in Switzerland than Coca-Cola. Difficult to describe to foreigners: a carbonated dairy drink that tastes nothing like dairy.

drinks.name: Fendant (Swiss White Wine)
ingredients: Fendant wine (Swiss Chasselas grape from Valais -- dry, mineral white wine)
instructions: Fendant is the Swiss white wine from the Valais canton -- the Alps wine
Made from the Chasselas grape -- called Fendant in Valais, Gutedel in Germany
The Valais: the Swiss Rhone Valley canton -- dramatic alpine scenery, terraced vineyards
The terraced Valais vineyards: built by hand from the Roman era, some of the steepest in Europe
Fendant character: light, dry, mineral, with a slight CO2 prickle -- refreshing
The slight carbonation (petillance) is a Chasselas characteristic
Fendant is the wine served with fondue -- the dry minerality cuts through the cheese fat
The legend: do not drink water with fondue -- the cheese will solidify in your stomach
Drink Fendant, or herbal tea, or kirsch -- never water
This legend is scientifically questionable but culturally unassailable
drinks.description: The Swiss alpine white wine -- Chasselas grape from the dramatically terraced Valais Rhone Valley vineyards, dry and mineral with a slight CO2 prickle (petillance). The natural pairing for fondue: the minerality cuts through the cheese fat. The fondue legend: never drink water with fondue (the cheese solidifies in your stomach). Drink Fendant, tea, or kirsch instead. Scientifically questionable; culturally unassailable.

drinks.name: Rivella or Appenzeller Alpenbitter (Digestif)
ingredients: Appenzeller Alpenbitter (Swiss herbal digestif liqueur -- 43 mountain herbs)
instructions: Appenzeller Alpenbitter is the Swiss herbal digestif -- from Appenzell canton
Made with 43 alpine herbs, roots, and spices -- the recipe is secret
Green and dark red (bitter) versions: the dark red is stronger and more bitter
Appenzell: the most traditional Swiss canton -- still uses the Landsgemeinde (open-air parliament)
The Alpenbitter is made to the same recipe for over 100 years
A shot after a heavy Swiss meal -- the 43 herbs aid digestion
The tradition of herbal digestifs in the Alps: the mountain pharmacopeia in a glass
Served neat and cold -- not mixed
The Appenzeller tradition: secrecy, quality, tradition -- like the cheese
drinks.description: Swiss alpine herbal digestif -- 43 mountain herbs, roots, and spices (secret recipe) distilled into a bitter liqueur from Appenzell canton, served neat and cold after a heavy Swiss meal. Appenzell is the most traditional Swiss canton, still using the open-air parliament (Landsgemeinde). The recipe is unchanged for over 100 years. The mountain pharmacopeia in a glass.
